t: Number of Squareful Arrays — Backtracking with Dedup and Bitmask DP
o: We must count permutations of `nums` where every adjacent pair sums to a perfect square. Since n ≤ 12, we can afford exponential search, but naive permutation generation (n! up to ~479M) is too slow without pruning. The key is to treat this as counting **Hamiltonian paths** in a graph where an edge exists between values whose sum is a perfect square. Duplicates matter: identical values are interchangeable, so we must count distinct value sequences, not index permutations. For example 1, [1,17,8]: valid edges are 1+8=9 and 8+17=25, giving paths [1,8,17] and [17,8,1] → answer 2. For example 2, [2,2,2]: all pairs sum to 4, but all permutations look identical as value sequences → answer 1.
k: Model the array as a graph: connect two values if their sum is a perfect square; the answer counts Hamiltonian paths in this multigraph.
Deduplicate by sorting and skipping repeated values at each recursion level (or fixing a canonical choice among equal elements), so identical values are not overcounted.
With n ≤ 12, bitmask DP over (used set, last element) gives O(2^n · n²) counting of Hamiltonian paths.

a.n: Approach 1: Backtracking with Sorting + Duplicate Skipping
a.i: Sort the array first so duplicates are adjacent. Build the permutation one position at a time; at each step try every unused value that forms a perfect-square sum with the previous element. Because the array is sorted, we skip a candidate equal to the previously tried candidate at the same level — this ensures each distinct value sequence is counted exactly once. The perfect-square check uses integer sqrt to avoid floating-point issues.
s: Sort nums and precompute nothing else; define used[] and a counter.
Backtrack(pos, prev): if pos == n, increment the count.
Iterate i from 0..n-1: skip if used[i], or if nums[i] == nums[i-1] and not used[i-1] (dedup), or if pos > 0 and nums[i] + prev is not a perfect square.
Mark used[i], recurse with prev = nums[i], unmark.
Start backtracking from every valid first element; return the count.
a.t: O(n!) worst case in theory, but perfect-square pruning and dedup make it fast in practice for n ≤ 12; the square check itself is O(1).
a.sp: O(n) for recursion depth and the used array (excluding input sorting).

a.n: Approach 2: Bitmask DP Counting Hamiltonian Paths
a.i: Precompute an adjacency matrix adj[i][j] = true when nums[i]+nums[j] is a perfect square. Let dp[mask][i] be the number of ways to build a valid sequence using exactly the indices in mask and ending at index i. Transitions extend any state ending at j where adj[j][i] holds. To handle duplicate values correctly, only start from the first occurrence of each value (mask with a single bit at its first index); then each distinct value sequence corresponds to exactly one index path, since among equal values we always pick the earliest available occurrence.
s: Build adjacency matrix adj on perfect-square sums.
Initialize dp[1<<i][i] = 1 only for the first occurrence of each distinct value.
For each mask in increasing order and each last index i with dp[mask][i] > 0, iterate unused j with adj[i][j]; add dp[mask][i] to dp[mask|1<<j][j].
Answer is the sum of dp[(1<<n)-1][i] over all i.
a.t: O(2^n · n²) — for each of 2^n masks we scan n ending positions and n next candidates; adjacency checks are precomputed.
a.sp: O(2^n · n) for the DP table plus O(n²) for the adjacency matrix.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1: it's natural, easy to explain, and passes comfortably given n ≤ 12 thanks to aggressive pruning. Mention Approach 2 (bitmask DP) as the guaranteed-polynomial-in-mask solution and implement it if asked for a bound better than factorial. Common pitfalls: (1) forgetting duplicate handling — [2,2,2] must yield 1, not 6; (2) floating-point sqrt errors near large sums up to 2·10^9 — use integer sqrt or adjust the rounded root; (3) treating permutations of equal values as distinct. Edge cases: single-element arrays (answer 1), arrays with no valid edges (answer 0), and zeros (0+x is a square only when x is a perfect square). Follow-ups: count squareful cycles instead of paths, or reconstruct one valid permutation.
